quote: Assumption 3.1. Suppose {X_1, ..., X_n} [{Y_1, ..., Y_n}] are n interdependent variables coupled with Archimedean (survival) copula with generator ψ_1 [ψ_2], where, for i = 1, ..., n, X_i ∼ Kw-G(x, α_i, γ_i; G) [Y_i ∼ Kw-G(x, β_i, δ_i; H)] and G [H] is the baseline distribution function. Further, let N_1 [N_2] be a positive integer-valued random variable independently of X'_i [Y'_i]. Also, let us denote r_g(x) = G'(x)/Ḡ(x) and r_h(x) = H'(x)/H̄(x). We start this section by the following theorem which states that under some sufficient conditions, if α ⪰^w β, then the random maxima X_{N_1:N_1} is stochastically larger than Y_{N_2:N_2}. Theorem 3.1. Let Assumption 3.1 hold with α, β ∈ E_+(D_+), γ = δ(≥ 1_n), G ≤ H. Also, suppose ϕ_2 ∘ ψ_1 is super-additive and ψ_1 or ψ_2 is log-concave. Then, α ⪰^w β ⇒ X_{N_1:N_1} ≥_st Y_{N_2:N_2}, whenever N_1 ≤_st N_2.
model: other: random maxima X_{N_1:N_1} vs Y_{N_2:N_2} (parallel systems with random numbers of dependent components)
family: Kumaraswamy-G family Kw-G(x, α, γ; G): F(x, α, γ) = 1 − (1 − G^α(x))^γ, α, γ > 0 (eq. (1.1)); X_i with baseline G, Y_i with baseline H; Archimedean copula generators ψ_1 (X) and ψ_2 (Y); F_{X_{N_1:N_1}}(x) = Σ_m P(X_{m:m} < x)P(N_1 = m), P(X_{n:n} < x) = ψ_1(Σ ϕ_1{1 − (1 − G^{α_i}(x))^{γ_i}})
compared: α vs β (first shape parameters), baselines G vs H, generators ψ_1 vs ψ_2, sample-size laws N_1 vs N_2; second shape parameters equal (γ = δ)

hypotheses.formal: X_1..X_n dependent via Archimedean copula (for maxima) with generator ψ_1, X_i ∼ Kw-G(α_i, γ_i; G); Y_i dependent with generator ψ_2, Y_i ∼ Kw-G(β_i, δ_i; H); N_1, N_2 positive integer-valued, independent of the X's and Y's respectively

hypotheses.text: Let ψ : [0, ∞) → [0, 1] be a non-increasing and continuous function, satisfying ψ(0) = 1 and ψ(∞) = 0 ... d monotone
hypotheses.formal: ψ_1, ψ_2 valid Archimedean generators, ϕ_k = ψ_k^{−1}
both α and β increasing (or both decreasing) ordered
G(x) ≤ H(x) for all x (not defined explicitly)
log ψ_1 or log ψ_2 concave
read as β ⪯^w α: Σ_{i=1}^l β_{i:n} ≥ Σ_{i=1}^l α_{i:n}, l = 1, ..., n
P(N_1 > m) ≤ P(N_2 > m) for all m

quote: Next, we consider a counterexample to show that the condition ψ_1 or ψ_2 is log-concave plays a crucial role for the result in Theorem 3.1 to hold. Counterexample 3.1. Let, X_i ∼ Kw-G(x, α_i, γ_i; G) and Y_i ∼ Kw-G(x, β_i, γ_i; H), for i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Set (γ_1, γ_2, γ_3, γ_4, γ_5) = (1.2, 1.5, 1.9, 2, 2.1), (α_1, α_2, α_3, α_4, α_5) = (1.1, 0.001, 0.0001, 0.00001, 0.00001) and (β_1, β_2, β_3, β_4, β_5) = (2.1, 3.001, 5.0001, 0.001, 0.0001). Clearly, (α_1, α_2, α_3, α_4, α_5) ⪰^w (β_1, β_2, β_3, β_4, β_5). Let G(x) = e^{−1/x} and H(x) = 1−e^{−x}, for x > 0. Also, let (X_1, X_2, X_3) be selected with probability P(N_1 = 3) = p(3) = 1/5, (X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4) be selected with probability P(N_1 = 4) = p(4) = 2/5 and, (X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4, X_5) be selected with probability P(N_1 = 5) = p(5) = 2/5; further let (Y_1, Y_2, Y_3) be selected with probability P(N_2 = 3) = p(3) = 1/5, (Y_1, Y_2, Y_3, Y_4) be selected with probability P(N_2 = 4) = p(4) = 3/5 and (Y_1, Y_2, Y_3, Y_4, Y_5) be selected with probability P(N_2 = 5) = p(5) = 1/5. Here, N_1 ≤_st N_2. Let us use the Gumbel copula with generators ψ_1(x) = e^{−x^{1/a}} and ψ_2(x) = e^{−x^{1/b}}, x > 0, with a = 2 and b = 2.1. Clearly, all the conditions are satisfied except ψ_1 and ψ_2 are log-concave. Figure 1(a) displays that the difference between F_{X_{N_1:N_1}}(x) and F_{Y_{N_2:N_2}}(x) crosses x axis, which violates the result in Theorem 3.1.
model: other: random maxima X_{N_1:N_1} vs Y_{N_2:N_2} (n = 5, random sizes N_1, N_2 ∈ {3, 4, 5})
family: Kw-G with baselines G(x) = e^{−1/x} (X) and H(x) = 1 − e^{−x} (Y), x > 0; Gumbel copula generators ψ_1(x) = e^{−x^{1/a}}, ψ_2(x) = e^{−x^{1/b}}, a = 2, b = 2.1

hypotheses.formal: asserted for the pmfs (1/5, 2/5, 2/5) and (1/5, 3/5, 1/5) on {3, 4, 5}

hypotheses.text: Clearly, all the conditions are satisfied except ψ_1 and ψ_2 are log-concave
hypotheses.formal: all hypotheses of Theorem 3.1 asserted except log-concavity of a generator

conclusion.direction: Theorem 3.1's conclusion X_{N_1:N_1} ≥_st Y_{N_2:N_2} fails (the cdf difference changes sign)

quantifiers: n = 5; x > 0 (Figure 1(a) plotted for x up to about 25)
numbers: γ = (1.2, 1.5, 1.9, 2, 2.1); α = (1.1, 0.001, 0.0001, 0.00001, 0.00001); β = (2.1, 3.001, 5.0001, 0.001, 0.0001); G(x) = e^{−1/x}; H(x) = 1 − e^{−x}; P(N_1 = 3, 4, 5) = 1/5, 2/5, 2/5; P(N_2 = 3, 4, 5) = 1/5, 3/5, 1/5; Gumbel a = 2, b = 2.1. Printed result: the difference between F_{X_{N_1:N_1}} and F_{Y_{N_2:N_2}} crosses the x axis. Figure 1(a) (legend F_{X_{N_1:N_1}}(x) − F_{Y_{N_2:N_2}}(x)) shows a curve rising from about −1.3 near x ≈ 0, crossing zero near x ≈ 2, and levelling at about 0.78.

Let Assumption 3.1 hold with α = β, α, γ, δ ∈ E_+(D_+) and G ≥ H. Also, suppose ϕ_2 ∘ ψ_1 is super-additive and ψ_1 or ψ_2 is log-convex. quote: Next, we present another counterexample to show that if we replace the condition 'G ≤ H' in Theorem 3.3 by 'G ≥ H', then the above theorem may not be true. Counterexample 3.2. Let, X_i ∼ Kw-G(x, α_i, γ_i; G) and Y_i ∼ Kw-G(x, α_i, δ_i; H), for i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Further, let (γ_1, γ_2, γ_3, γ_4, γ_5) = (3.9, 3.1, 2.9, 2.8, 2.1), (δ_1, δ_2, δ_3, δ_4, δ_5) = (3.2, 2.6, 1.9, 1.2, 1) and (α_1, α_2, α_3, α_4, α_5) = (β_1, β_2, β_3, β_4, β_5) = (0.01, 7, 9, 9.1, 9.12). Clearly, (γ_1, γ_2, γ_3, γ_4, γ_5) ⪰_w (δ_1, δ_2, δ_3, δ_4, δ_5). Let G(x) = e^{−1/x} and H(x) = 1 − e^{−x}, for x > 0. Also, let (X_1, X_2, X_3) be selected with probability P(N_1 = 3) = p(3) = 1/5, (X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4) be selected with probability P(N_1 = 4) = p(4) = 2/5 and (X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4, X_5) be selected with probability P(N_1 = 5) = p(5) = 2/5; further let (Y_1, Y_2, Y_3) be selected with probability P(N_2 = 3) = p(3) = 1/5, (Y_1, Y_2, Y_3, Y_4) be selected with probability P(N_2 = 4) = p(4) = 3/5 and (Y_1, Y_2, Y_3, Y_4, Y_5) be selected with probability P(N_2 = 5) = p(5) = 1/5. Here, N_1 ≤_st N_2. Consider the Gumbel copula with generators ψ_1(x) = e^{−x^{1/a}} and ψ_2(x) = e^{−x^{1/b}}, x > 0, with a = 1.4 and b = 2.5. Here, all the conditions of Theorem 3.3 are satisfied except G ≥ H. Figure 1(b) displays the difference between F̄_{X_{1:N_1}}(x) and F̄_{Y_{1:N_2}}(x) crosses x axis for some x ≥ 0, which violates the statement of Theorem 3.3.

quote: The following counterexample shows that the log-convexity condition is required for Theorem 3.4. Counterexample 3.3. Suppose X_i ∼ Kw-G(x, α_i, γ_i; G) and Y_i ∼ Kw-G(x, α_i, δ_i; H), for i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Further, let (α_1, α_2, α_3, α_4, α_5) = (7.1, 2.9, 1.56, 0.03, 0.201), (β_1, β_2, β_3, β_4, β_5) = (8.1, 3.009, 2.6, 1.06, 0.01) and (γ_1, γ_2, γ_3, γ_4, γ_5) = (δ_1, δ_2, δ_3, δ_4, δ_5) = (5.02, 2.05, 1.09, 0.01, 0.001). It is easy to see that (α_1, α_2, α_3, α_4, α_5) ⪰^w (β_1, β_2, β_3, β_4, β_5). Let H(x) = e^{−1/x} and G(x) = 1 − e^{−x}, for x > 0. Also, let (X_1, X_2, X_3) be selected with probability P(N_1 = 3) = p(3) = 1/5, (X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4) be selected with probability P(N_1 = 4) = p(4) = 2/5 and (X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4, X_5) be selected with probability P(N_1 = 5) = p(5) = 2/5; further, let (Y_1, Y_2, Y_3) be selected with probability P(N_2 = 3) = p(3) = 1/5, (Y_1, Y_2, Y_3, Y_4) be selected with probability P(N_2 = 4) = p(4) = 3/5 and (Y_1, Y_2, Y_3, Y_4, Y_5) be selected with probability P(N_2 = 5) = p(5) = 1/5, which satisfy the condition N_1 ≤_st N_2. Choose the Gumbel-Hougaard copula with generators ψ_1(x) = e^{1−(1+x)^{1/a}} and ψ_2(x) = e^{1−(1+x)^{1/b}}, x > 0, with a = 4.0002 and b = 4.0001. So, all the conditions of Theorem 3.4 are satisfied except the log-convexity of ψ_1 and ψ_2. Figure 2 displays the difference between F̄_{X_{1:N_1}}(x) and F̄_{Y_{1:N_2}}(x) crosses x axis for some x ≥ 0. Therefore, Theorem 3.4 can not be possible without the log-convexity property of the generators.

claim: Section 4.1 application (first activation scheme, via Theorem 3.1 as printed)
quote: Under the above set up, we assume that the failure times of the cells are interdependently distributed as Kw-W with CDF of the ith cell being G(x) = 1 − [1 − {1 − exp^{−(ηx)^λ}}^{α_i}]^{γ_i}, x, α_i, γ_i, λ, η > 0, for i = 1, ..., n. Here, we consider Weibull distribution as the parent CDF of the Kw-G distribution. Now, let us assume two cancer patients who are under a treatment. Suppose {X_1, ..., X_n} are the incubation times for the n carcinogenic cells and N_1 is the number of carcinogenic cells that are left active for the first patient after first chemotherapy, where X_i ∼ Kw- W(x, α_i, γ_i, η, λ) and N_1 ∼ Poission(λ_1). Similarly, for the second patient, let {Y_1, ..., Y_n} be the incubation times for the n carcinogenic cells and N_2 be the number of carcinogenic cells that are left active, where Y_i ∼ Kw- W(x, β_i, δ_i, η, ζ) and N_2 ∼ Poission(λ_2). Then, under the given setup, by using Theorem 3.1 (Theorem 3.4), we can say that the failure time of the first (last) activation scheme for the first patient is more (less) than that of the second patient when the shape parameters α and β are connected by weakly-supermajorization order.

quote: Under the above setting, let us consider the random accident-free distances X_i, for i = 1, ..., n, to be interdependently distributed as Kw-E with CDF of the ith component being G(x) = 1−[1−{1−exp^{−(λx)}}^{α_i}]^{γ_i}, x, α_i, γ_i, λ > 0. Here, we consider the exponential distribution as the parent CDF of the Kw-G distribution. Suppose two types of explosives (i) Type A and (ii) Type B are being shifted from one place to another. Let {X_1, ..., X_{N_1}} represent the random accident-free distances corresponding to each defective (Type A) and N_1 be the number of defective units that could explode, where X_i ∼ Kw- E(x, α_i, γ_i, µ_1) and N_1 ∼ Poission(λ_1). Also, let {Y_1, ..., Y_{N_2}} represent the random accident-free distances corresponding to each defective (Type B) and N_2 be the number of defectives that could explode, where Y_i ∼ Kw- E(x, β_i, δ_i, µ_2) and N_2 ∼ Poission(µ_2). Then, under the given setup, using Theorem 3.4, one can easily state that the accident free distance of Type A shipment is less than that of Type B when the shape parameters α and β are connected by weakly-supermajorization order. Similar interpretations can be provided for other theorems as well.
